overview: This record follows Taiwan from the end of Japanese rule through authoritarian government and democratization. Modern Taiwan governs itself as the Republic of China; its international status remains disputed. The atlas outline cannot decide that dispute.

periods.title: Postwar administration
periods.summary: The Republic of China took over administration after Japan’s defeat; the February 28 Incident followed in 1947.

periods.title: Authoritarian rule and social change
periods.summary: The ROC government relocated to Taiwan in 1949. Martial law restricted political activity while public institutions and industry developed.

periods.title: Democratic transition
periods.summary: Martial law ended in Taiwan and Penghu in 1987; military administration in Kinmen and Matsu continued until 1992.

periods.title: Direct presidential elections
periods.summary: Voters first directly elected the president in 1996.

periods.title: Democracy and continuing debate
periods.summary: Peaceful transfers between parties followed the 2000 presidential election. The political status question remained unresolved.

sections.title: A modern history with a complicated map

items.text: The atlas begins in 1945, not at the founding of a new Taiwanese nation. Its five snapshots show a generalized main island and omit Penghu, Kinmen, Matsu, Green Island and Orchid Island. The 1994 coastline even misses the tested Hualien city point. These are cartographic limits, not declarations about sovereignty, identity or present-day control.

After Japan’s defeat in 1945, the Republic of China administered Taiwan. In 1949, after defeat in the Chinese Civil War, the ROC central government relocated to the island. The National Human Rights Museum dates martial law in Taiwan from May 1949 and describes arrests, wrongful convictions and political repression under Kuomintang rule.

The February 28 Incident of 1947 left memories that official paperwork alone could not capture. For its seventieth anniversary in 2017, the National Museum of Taiwan History assembled documents and relics contributed by memorial organizations and families’ cultural foundations. Exhibitions can help make silenced experiences part of a shared historical conversation.

Green Island, off the east coast and absent from this atlas polygon, preserves prisons associated with the White Terror. Oasis Villa’s central eight-sided structure overlooked four corridors. Today the museum uses the buildings and explanatory models to teach about imprisonment, forced work and re-education. An ordinary floor plan can reveal how authorities watched and controlled people.

Political opening also changed family life. The Presidential Office’s historical account records that 1987 brought permission for visits to relatives on the mainland as well as the lifting of martial law. Political separation had personal consequences: the ability to travel could mean seeing family again.

Democratization came in stages. Taiwan held a full direct Legislative Yuan election in 1992 and its first direct presidential election in 1996. In 2000 the presidency changed peacefully between parties. Voting institutions replaced an earlier system in which one ruling party tightly controlled political life.

The Congressional Research Service’s August 2025 account describes Taiwan as a self-governing democracy, formally called the Republic of China, administering Taiwan and outlying islands. The People’s Republic of China claims Taiwan. Actual government, diplomatic recognition and sovereignty claims are different questions; a colored atlas polygon cannot answer all three.

Taiwan’s semiconductor industry grew through deliberate learning as well as invention. ITRI’s 2023 retrospective describes a 1976 technology agreement with the American company RCA. Nineteen engineers trained in different specialties: circuit design, manufacturing, verification and equipment. Making tiny chips required a surprisingly large collection of skills.

In 1987 ITRI helped create TSMC by transferring manufacturing facilities, equipment, technologies and ninety-eight professionals. This was institution-building, not a lone inventor producing a chip in a shed. Laboratories, trained workers and factories connected research to an industry supplying electronic components.

Schooling expanded over generations. Nine-year compulsory education began in the 1968 school year: six years of primary school and three of junior high. The twelve-year basic education framework introduced in 2014 added a broader path through senior secondary education. The Ministry of Education distinguishes this framework from the nine legally compulsory years.

Learning also means keeping languages alive. In Taipei’s Nangang District, a 2024 holiday course offered Indigenous children aged three to six opportunities to learn languages and cultures. The program included Siraya and Taokas material and planned songs, dance, children’s creations and parent-child activities. This named urban program reflects diversity that a single label such as “Taiwanese” can hide.

A banknote can turn a pocket into a miniature classroom. The blue thousand-dollar note issued in July 2005 depicts primary-school children on the front and a Mikado pheasant with Yushan on the back. The issuing bank’s announcement also describes a holographic strip and color-changing ink: the pictures teach, while the printing helps discourage counterfeiting.

Raohe Street Night Market in Taipei’s Songshan District offers a concrete taste of urban food culture. The city’s tourism guide lists pepper meat buns, oyster vermicelli, herbal pork-rib soup, duck and stinky tofu. The menu can turn an evening stroll into several small meals; its strongly scented tofu announces itself before the first bite.

Some garbage trucks have a soundtrack. A 2016 Ministry of Culture account described the familiar tunes “Für Elise” and “A Maiden’s Prayer” and an approved project to prepare Hakka orchestral songs for Longtan’s trucks. The music accompanies the system of bringing waste to collection vehicles. Taking out the rubbish can come with a concert cue.

Family law changed too. A law promulgated in May 2019 made same-sex marriage possible from May 24 that year. The reform followed a constitutional-court decision and legislative debate. It gave same-sex couples a legal route to marriage; it did not mean that everyone’s experiences or all family-law questions immediately became identical.

sections.title: Health, clean surroundings and everyday technology

items.text: National Health Insurance began on March 1, 1995. It brought health coverage into a compulsory, premium-financed, single-payer system, replacing a fragmented landscape of job-based insurance schemes. The reform mattered at the scale of an ordinary family: access to healthcare was no longer organized only around which occupation supplied an insurance plan.

In January 2004 the insurance authority replaced paper health-insurance cards with smart cards. The card connected patients, providers and the insurer through an information network. A small object in a wallet became part of the machinery behind a clinic visit.

A 1986 public-health report documents an important early hepatitis B program. Beginning in July 1984, pregnant women were screened and infants born to infected mothers were offered vaccination. The report measured how many mothers and babies the program reached. It shows prevention becoming a coordinated service for families, rather than waiting for illness to appear.

Toilets have a history of changing habits. Guidelines revised in August 2025 promoted flushing appropriate amounts of dispersible toilet paper instead of putting it in waste bins. The environmental authority carefully distinguished it from wet wipes, paper towels and other items that can clog pipes. A toilet is useful engineering, but it is not a rubbish chute.

The same public-restroom program promotes more sitting toilets for people whose knees or mobility make squatting difficult, while retaining squatting options. It also calls for cleaning supplies and better facilities. This is a stated improvement policy, not proof that every restroom is already equally accessible.

The thousand-dollar note introduced on July 20, 2005 carries “壹仟圓” ,  yī qiān yuán, “one thousand dollars.” The Central Bank’s issue announcement explicitly transcribes these Traditional Chinese characters beside the numeral 1000. This is a securely dated modern monetary inscription, given here in the issuer’s transcription; Chinese writing is one part of Taiwan’s multilingual life.

ending.text: Taiwan’s self-government continues, while its international status remains disputed. Democratization changed its institutions; its diverse communities continue.
